newsitem.title: FRANCE: Lebed warns of Russia protests for election.
newsitem.headline: Lebed warns of Russia protests for election.

text.p: Russians could follow the lead of Bulgarians and stage protests to force an early election, according to Alexander Lebed, the favourite if presidential elections were held now in Russia.

The 46-year-old former Russian security chief and paratroop general told the French weekly Paris Match in an interview published on Wednesday the Bulgarians' patience was second only to that of the Russians.
"They (Bulgarians) exploded. The Russians will follow suit," he said.
Month-long protests forced Sofia's Socialist government to call an election for April, 20 months ahead of schedule.

Pressure for new presidential elections has been mounting in Russia amid doubts that ailing President Boris Yeltsin could rule effectively. He underwent a quintuple heart bypass after being re-elected last July and is recovering from pneumonia.

Lebed, who has firmly set his sights on the presidency, said violence could sweep Russia if the government tried to change the constitution to have the president chosen by parliament rather than by a popular vote.
"There are indications that the rulers are prepared to overtly flout the Constitution. They are obviously prepared to trample it underfoot," he said.

"The people, 80 percent of whom live in extreme poverty, would be deprived of their last right, that of choosing their president," he said, adding that if this happened, "there will be a great and tough battle".
Lebed fell out with Yeltsin after helping him to election victory. He was sacked after forging a deal to end the war in Chechnya during his brief spell as national security chief.
He told Paris Match he would never again work with Yeltsin and was certain of winning the presidency sooner or later.
Lebed cautioned the West against antagonising Russia through plans to enlarge NATO to eastern European countries.
He said enlarging the Atlantic alliance could trigger a new arms race and peripheral Russian regions could be tempted to turn towards the United States, China, Germany or Japan.
"This would cause a new sharing out of the world. And sharing out the world means waging a war which we know no-one will win," he said.
"This is the reason why I am calling on all countries to take care of Russia... because, if it were to be destroyed, it would bury you under its rubble," he said.

Lebed said NATO's structures should be re-deployed to face the 21st century's major hazards: terrorism, including nuclear terrorism, technological disasters, drug-trafficking, the ozone layer, the earth's global warming up.

"We must think how to use NATO's well-oiled structures to prevent these major hazards. It will be necessary to first change the organisation's very name...which remains as a thorn from the Cold War," he said.
